10         RELATES TO THE TESTIMONY OF MR. DAVID GARRETT.

11   A.    My rebuttal testimony responds to Mr. David Garrett’s proposals for different

12         service life and net salvage estimates recommended by the Company. Mr. Garrett’s

13         service life proposals are based primarily, if not entirely, on comparing

14         mathematical results from the statistical life analysis contained in the depreciation

15         study that I sponsor in my direct testimony. However, as clearly explained by

16         depreciation authorities, such as the National Association of Regulatory Utility

17         Commissioners (NARUC), estimating service lives must necessarily include a

18         subjective component. Service life estimates are a forecast of the future and

19         focusing only on mathematical calculations based on historical data will lead to

13        Mr. Garrett’s overall approach differs from mine. His approach also differs from the

14        correct and proper approach to estimating service lives that is set forth in depreciation

15        textbooks such as NARUC’s Public Utility Depreciation Practices. Specifically, Mr.

16        Garrett’s testimony indicates that he believes estimating service lives is primarily a

17        mathematical exercise for which little more than mathematical computations of

18        historical data will result in reasonable estimates. This overall approach is incorrect.

 3            WHICH SERVICE LIFE ESTIMATES SHOULD BE DETERMINED?

 4   A.       Yes. In his testimony, Mr. Garrett says, “Mathematical fitting is an important part of

 5            the curve-fitting process because it promotes objective, unbiased results.”1 He goes on

 6            to acknowledge that, “While mathematical curve fitting is important, however, it may

 7            not always yield the optimum result; therefore, it should not necessarily be adopted

 8            without further analysis.”2 Mr. Garrett’s testimony then presents the reasoning behind

 9            each of his service life estimates which appear to be based solely on the mathematical

10            curve fitting of the historical data. He mentions no other considerations for his

11            selections besides the “substantial increase to depreciation expense proposed by

12            EPE.”3 On first glance, it may appear that a mathematical result is more reliable and

13            removes the uncertainty of estimating service lives; however, the objectivity sought by

14            Mr. Garrett is neither realistic nor desirable in the development of a true forecast of the

15            future. Using a strictly mathematical approach on a stub curve as is the case for many

16            of the accounts clearly contradicts his objectivity component and ignores the key

17            concept that the survivor curve should represent the full life characteristics of the assets

18            within an account.

 1                    Authorities on the topic of depreciation, such as NARUC, are clear that

 5           “Actuarial analysis objectively measures how the company has retired its investment.

 6           The analyst must then judge whether this historical view depicts the future life of the

 7           property in service. The analyst takes into consideration various factors, such as

 8           changes in technology, services provided, or capital budgets.”4 NARUC further states,

 9           “Depreciation analysts should avoid becoming ensnared in the mechanics of the

 3   Q15. HOW DO YOU APPROACH THE CURVE FITTING PROCESS?

 4   A.   In my professional opinion, both mathematical and visual curve fitting should be used.

 5        Employing both approaches enhances the information available to the analyst and aids

 6        in developing the most reasonable forecast. Importantly, the analyst should also

 7        understand the advantages and disadvantages of both approaches so not to be misled

 8        by the results. The mathematical approach assumes the future will be identical to the

 9        past and all assets, regardless of age and value, are the same. We know this is not true

10        and more importantly, we know that there will be different forces of retirement in the

11        future than what have occurred in the past. The visual approach does not take into

12        consideration trends or change in asset mix. Therefore, a combination of both methods

13        is necessary.

14

15   Q16. ARE THERE DIFFERENCES IN THE MATHEMATICAL CURVE

16        FITTING PERFORMED BY MR. DAVID GARRETT AND BY YOU?

17   A.   Yes. While we both generally use a sum of squares difference (SSD) approach to

18        calculate mathematical curve fitting indicators, there is one distinction that I believe

19        adds value to my approach. Mr. Garrett simply sums the squares of difference to arrive

20        at the numbers he cites in his testimony. However, this approach does not normalize

21        the mathematical curve fitting indicators to the number of data points included. My


                                                 8
                                 EL PASO ELECTRIC COMPANY
                                 REBUTTAL TESTIMONY OF
                                      JOHN J. SPANOS

 1       mathematical results incorporate this normalization aspect to develop a figure referred

 2       to as the residual measure. As with the SSD, the smaller the residual measure, the

 3       better the mathematical fit. Additionally, Mr. Garrett’s mathematical calculations give

 4       the same weight to a very old asset with little value as a new asset with high value that

 5       will be in service for many years to come.

 6               Mr. Garrett also references using a 1% of exposures threshold to perform

 7       additional mathematical curve fitting. The practice of a 1% of exposures threshold is

 8       only appropriate if you understand the assets that survived beyond the 1% threshold. I

 9       often analyze this threshold for mathematical curve matching as well, but that does not

10       mean that it should be used systematically on every account. The mechanical process

11       of cutting every observed life table (OLT) curve at 1% of exposures and choosing the

12       best mathematical fit to those data points is not an appropriate way to conduct life

13       analysis. The 1% cutoff is simply a general guideline that can be explored and analyzed

14       by the analyst when deciding where to make a T-Cut of the OLT curve. Further, while

15       Mr. Garrett claims to not rely solely on mathematical results in choosing his curves,

16       his only justification for his selected curves are that they have a lower SSD compared

17       with the historical data than the estimates proposed in the depreciation study.

 1   Q26. WHAT         IS    THE     DRIVER        FOR     THE      COMPANY’S          PROPOSED

 2          ADJUSTMENTS TO RETIREMENT DATES IN THIS CASE?

 3   A.     As stated in Part III of the depreciation study, probable retirement dates are not

 4          commitments to retire facilities at the estimated dates. They are estimates that mark

 5          key decision-making points where the future viability of production units must be

 6          assessed. Probable retirement dates are typically based on the expected need to either

 7          retire or repower a facility, because continuing the operational status quo beyond that

 8          date is no longer an option. Continued operation of such facilities requires significant

 9          investment. This is the case for the facilities with proposed retirement date revisions

10          in this case. New Mexico’s Renewable Energy Act requirements will be a driver of

11          the decisions made for these plants. Even if details of the zero carbon by 2045 goal are

12          not yet clear, it is clear that status quo operation of these plants beyond 2045 is highly

13          unlikely and planning to depreciate them in the same manner beyond 2045 would be

14          poor planning.
